name: PayToSpeak
one_liner: Clubhouse on Monad: every few seconds the room micro-auctions who gets the next line on the big screen.
mechanic: A QR opens a tiny bid sheet (embedded wallet / session key). Every ~3 seconds a new speaking slot Dutch-auctions down; highest bidder's short text (max 40 chars, client wordfilter) locks to the projector when the auction's end block finalizes. Only active bidders hit the network—typically a handful per round, not 167. A rotating set of 8–12 funded relayer wallets submit bids to avoid single-wallet nonce meltdown; the projector lists open auction, top bid, and confirmed speaker as separate lanes.
why_monad: You need fast blocks so a live auction can open, clear, and display speech inside a breath. Parallelism is honest: independent bidder intents and multiple relayer wallets, with pending vs confirmed bid rows on screen. Do not show a TPS counter; show auction cadence (slots cleared per minute) and explorer links for each winning bid.
room_participation: Anyone who wants the mic scans once and spam-bids a meme line; the rest of the room reads the winning messages on the projector as the pitch continues.
build_plan_6h45: Contract: SpeakAuction with commitBid, settleSlot, cooldown per address. Frontend: mobile bid UI + projector ticker. Infra: Privy/Sequence gasless for bidders, 8 server relayers with local nonces, HTTPS deploy. Stub: host can seed 3 canned winning lines if Wi-Fi is bad; fall back to stage-tablet bidding for four volunteers.
biggest_risk: Venue Wi-Fi plus RPC limits during bid bursts; cap bids/second/client, rotate relayers across two RPC providers (public endpoints are rate-limited—QuickNode ~25 rps, Alchemy ~15 rps), and keep the stage-tablet fallback warm.
novelty_vs_corpus: Chat/messaging has a 14.3% win rate, but prior candidates were ephemeral chat feeds (Ephemera/Signal Stream), not a live pay-to-speak auction for the room screen. It is recognisable (Clubhouse/Twitter Spaces) without copying a past winner.

name: Overheard at Blitz
one_liner: Yik Yak for the hackathon: an anonymous, uncensorable confession board living entirely on Monad — post from a burner key, tip MON to push the best gossip to the top.
mechanic: QR stickers hit every table at 13:00. The web app mints an anonymous burner key; posts go on-chain as calldata events, so the feed IS the chain — no database, no admin, no delete button. Anyone can tip MON to a post, and the feed ranks by tip-weighted recency, so the room curates its own front page all afternoon ('the sponsor pizza is gone', 'table 9 is vibe-coding in prod', 'someone just deployed to mainnet by accident'). The venue screen cycles the top confessions between now and the pitches.
why_monad: A social feed served purely from chain state only works with Monad's economics: a post is a few hundred bytes of calldata costing a fraction of a cent, confirmed in 800ms, so the feed refreshes like a Web2 app with no backend — which we prove by killing our server live during the pitch and reloading the whole feed from a public RPC read. Honest scale, honestly framed: dozens of posts and tips over five hours at natural rate, no rate-limit stress, no synthetic load, and every confession's tx hash is one tap away.
room_participation: They already used it all afternoon — the pitch replays the day's top 10 confessions in their own words, huge on screen, then runs one live round: 'post what you really think of this pitch.' New posts and tips appear and re-rank the feed on the big screen within a second.
build_plan_6h45: Contract (1h): Board.sol — post(bytes) and tip(postId) payable, events only, no storage arrays. Frontend (3h): mobile feed with burner-key generation, compose, tip button, tip-weighted ranking, big-screen ticker mode, and a backend-free read path via getLogs. Infra (0.75h): gasless-post relayer plus optional key dusting, QR stickers printed at lunch, 20 quality seed confessions. Stubbed: client-side profanity filter only, no images, no replies — tipping is the entire interaction model.
biggest_risk: Content risk — an anonymous board can go quiet or go feral; mitigated by seeding, the visible tip-to-top incentive, and the client-side filter, but a dead feed at pitch time would sting.
novelty_vs_corpus: Chat/messaging runs a 14.3% win rate with only 7 entries ever and zero anonymous-social projects in the 1,327. Unlike generic socialfi clones this is hyperlocal to the event itself, so by voting time it is the room's shared in-joke — the only project whose demo content was written by the voters themselves.

name: Proof of Jump
one_liner: Bitcoin mining powered by the room doing jumping jacks, with every camera-detected burst filling an onchain block.
mechanic: A stage webcam divides the audience image into a grid and measures local motion energy without identifying faces. The screen gives the room 30 seconds to mine a ceremonial Monad block by jumping, waving and moving until the target is reached. Each validated grid pulse advances a visible mining bar and lights its cell only after the transaction confirms. When the target is hit, the contract emits a block-found event and unlocks a commemorative claim QR.
why_monad: Dozens of camera zones can emit updates every 400ms, with each zone writing to independent epoch state so parallel execution matters. Recording sensor pulses individually would be impractical on a slow chain but creates an immediate block-by-block spectacle on Monad. The projector overlays confirmed cells, block numbers, receipts per block and finality latency directly on the live camera feed.
room_participation: Nobody needs Wi-Fi for the core demo: the presenter asks the entire room to stand or wave, then everyone physically moves together for 30 seconds to fill the mining bar.
build_plan_6h45: Use a browser webcam, OpenCV.js frame differencing and a fixed 8-by-6 motion grid rather than fragile multi-person pose recognition. Deploy a Solidity mining contract with per-zone cooldowns, epoch totals, target completion and an ERC-1155 claim token. Feed detections through 16 relayer lanes and render a camera heatmap plus receipt confirmations in Next.js. Stub identity, exact repetition counting and token economics; calibrate thresholds in the venue before pitches.
biggest_risk: Lighting, camera angle or audience reluctance can weaken detection; use large grid zones, an adjustable threshold and waving as an accessible fallback to jumping.
novelty_vs_corpus: Mojoman counted and bet on individual exercise performances; this turns anonymous whole-room motion into parallel onchain mining, requires no audience phones and has no betting mechanic.

name: Block Blitz
one_liner: WarioWare for 167 phones: the whole room taps, tilts and shakes through three 12-second onchain challenges.
mechanic: A QR code opens an instant session-key controller with no login or wallet popup. Players complete three rapid rounds: reaction tapping, tilting a ball into a target and shaking to charge a meter. Each scored action becomes a signed intent, while the projector shows teams, live receipts and a final room leaderboard. The entire game fits inside 45 seconds, leaving time to celebrate the winning row of the room.
why_monad: Hundreds of simultaneous actions are preserved as individual transactions rather than hidden in one batch, producing visible bursts across 400ms blocks. Player and round state occupy independent storage slots suited to parallel execution. The projector groups confirmed actions by block and displays transaction count, block hash and measured submission-to-finality latency.
room_participation: Everyone scans one QR, enters a nickname, then taps, tilts and shakes their phone during the three rounds; the winning player and winning side of the room appear live.
build_plan_6h45: Deploy one Solidity round-and-score contract accepting EIP-712 intents, with replay protection and events. Build a Next.js controller plus Canvas projector, using browser motion APIs and WebSockets for immediate animation. Run 16 pre-funded relayer keys across two RPC endpoints and reconcile every animation against receipts. Stub sophisticated anti-cheat, matchmaking and permanent profiles; ship only three polished minigames.
biggest_risk: Venue Wi-Fi and iOS motion-permission friction; provide a tap-only fallback and let already-open clients keep playing if sensor permission fails.
novelty_vs_corpus: The corpus has onchain arcades, but no project makes the entire audience the simultaneous controller or packages high-frequency phone sensors as a rapid WarioWare show.

name: Finality Bet
one_liner: Binary prediction market on a physical event resolving within 800ms finality window.
mechanic: Host performs action (e.g., card flip). Audience bets YES/NO. Contract settles instantly after oracle submission.
why_monad: 800ms finality allows the bet to open, close, and settle during the 2-minute pitch, impossible on slower L1s.
room_participation: Audience places bets via QR while host prepares the physical event.
build_plan_6h45: Simple YesNo contract + Oracle signer (host's phone). Frontend shows odds updating. Use Permit2 for one-click betting.
biggest_risk: Oracle delay or dispute; mitigated by host being trusted signer for demo.
novelty_vs_corpus: Hunch was digital outcomes; this ties physical reality to chain speed directly during the pitch.

name: ShakePay
one_liner: Accelerometer-driven NFT minting where physical intensity determines rarity.
mechanic: Web app reads phone accelerometer. Shake intensity > threshold triggers mint. Rarity tier based on G-force peak.
why_monad: High TPS allows hundreds of mints in seconds without gas spike congestion; cheap blocks enable micro-mints.
room_participation: Everyone stands up and shakes phones for 30 seconds; screen shows live mint feed.
build_plan_6h45: ERC721 contract + React app using DeviceMotion API. Use CreateX for deployment. Stub rarity logic with simple Math.max.
biggest_risk: iOS/Android browser permissions blocking sensor access without native wrapper.
novelty_vs_corpus: Mojoman used cameras (privacy friction); this uses sensors (privacy-safe) focusing on kinetic energy vs pose.

name: Reverse Turk
one_liner: Mechanical Turk, inverted: an autonomous AI agent with its own budget hires the room as gig workers and pays real MON to your phone within a second of your work being accepted.
mechanic: An LLM agent holds a funded Monad wallet and a goal (during the pitch: 'caption this photo of the venue' or 'rank these five logo drafts'). It posts micro-tasks to a job board; anyone who scanned the QR has an instant browser wallet, taps to accept, and submits an answer. The agent auto-grades submissions against a rubric and calls the escrowed Payroll contract, which pushes an individual transfer to each approved worker — payouts hit worker addresses in under a second and their phones show the balance tick up. The escrow means the agent cannot stiff workers, and a big-screen payroll ticker shows total wages paid and top earners.
why_monad: The on-screen claim is instant sub-cent micro-payroll, not audience TPS: there is one honest payer — the agent, which IS the product — making a few hundred individually visible transfers with 800ms finality, so payroll receipts appear on monadscan while the worker is still holding their phone up. Paying humans per-task at fraction-of-a-penny wages is only economical at Monad-class fees, and the accept→grade→paid loop only feels magical at sub-second finality. Nothing is proxied or simulated: every payout is a real transfer to a key only that attendee controls, and workers verify their own tx hash live.
room_participation: QR → instant wallet → the agent posts one 30-second task to the whole room; ~100 answers stream onto the screen, the agent grades the best 50 live and fires payroll; everyone who got paid watches MON land on their own address and shows their neighbour, while the wage ticker climbs on the big screen.
build_plan_6h45: Contract (1h): Payroll escrow — fund, batched approve-and-pay(worker[], amount[]), refund. Agent (2h): Claude API loop — post task, collect submissions through a small API, grade with a fixed rubric prompt, trigger payout via viem. Frontend (2.5h): worker mobile page (task feed, submit, live balance) and boss dashboard / big-screen ticker. Infra (0.5h): dedicated RPC, agent wallet funding. Stubbed: one task type live (short text answers), no dispute flow, machine-to-machine x402 mode described in the README but not built.
biggest_risk: Grading latency — LLM-scoring 100 submissions inside the pitch window; mitigated by streaming grades as answers arrive and paying in two waves so the first payouts land within 30 seconds of the task posting.
novelty_vs_corpus: All 84 x402/agentic-payment entries in the corpus point money agent→merchant or agent→API; none makes humans the payees. It inverts the ecosystem's house theme, and unlike winner Monacle (agent buys plush toys) the room is not watching commerce happen — each voter personally gets paid during the pitch.

name: HeartChain
one_liner: Live room-wide heart rate competition using phone cameras, with on-chain bets settled in real time.
mechanic: Attendees open a web app, place their phone camera on their finger, and the app uses photoplethysmography (PPG) to detect their pulse. They join a 60-second competition to achieve the lowest resting heart rate. A smart contract records hashed heart rate submissions and settles bets placed on who will win. A live leaderboard on the big screen updates as measurements stream in.
why_monad: Monad's 10,000 TPS and parallel execution handle dozens of simultaneous heart rate submissions and independent bet settlements without congestion. 400ms block times ensure the leaderboard updates near-instantly, making the competition feel live and responsive.
room_participation: During the 2-minute pitch, the presenter asks everyone to pull out their phones, open the app, and place a finger on the camera. The big screen shows a live leaderboard of heart rates and bet odds. The room cheers as the lowest heart rate emerges, and winners are paid out on the spot.
build_plan_6h45: Smart contract: Foundry project with a bet pool and heart rate submission (hashed) contract. Frontend: Next.js app using a PPG library (e.g., rPPG) for camera-based pulse detection. Infra: Privy embedded wallets for gasless transactions, a relayer to batch submissions and avoid nonce contention. Stub: No real identity verification; trust that submissions are honest (or use a simple anti-spam).
biggest_risk: Venue Wi-Fi may struggle with 167 simultaneous camera streams and transactions. Mitigation: Use a single relayer wallet to submit batched heart rate updates, reducing RPC calls. Camera access may be denied by some users; provide a fallback manual entry option.
novelty_vs_corpus: While fitness/IRL sensor projects have a high win rate, none of the 1,327 past projects combined live heart rate sensing with a room-wide competition and on-chain betting. Mojoman used pose detection for exercise reps; HeartChain uses a different biometric and a simpler, more inclusive mechanic.

name: MetaPulse
one_liner: A prediction market platform for the hackathon itself, where the audience bets on live outcomes during the pitch.
mechanic: A platform where anyone can create a binary prediction market about the event (e.g., 'Will the Wi-Fi crash?', 'Will project X win?'). Markets are resolved manually by the organizer. During the pitch, the presenter creates a market, and the audience places bets from their phones. Odds update in real time, and payouts are settled instantly after resolution.
why_monad: Monad's fast finality (800ms) allows near-instant bet settlement, and parallel execution handles many independent bets without congestion. The high TPS ensures that odds update smoothly even with 167 simultaneous bettors.
room_participation: The presenter shows a live market on the big screen. The audience opens the app, picks a side, and bets. They watch the odds shift as more people join. At the end of the pitch, the market is resolved, and winners see their payouts immediately.
build_plan_6h45: Smart contract: A simple fixed-product AMM for binary markets, with a resolve function callable by the owner. Frontend: Next.js app with market creation and betting UI. Use Privy for embedded wallets and a relayer for gasless transactions. Stub: Oracle is manual (organizer resolves). Use the foundry-monad template.
biggest_risk: Regulatory perception, but on testnet it's low-risk. Wi-Fi issues could delay bet placement; use optimistic UI. Market resolution requires trust in the organizer; for the demo, it's acceptable.
novelty_vs_corpus: Prediction markets are common (10.9% win rate), but MetaPulse is specifically designed for live, in-room event betting during the pitch itself. It differs from Hunch (a single timed game) by being a full market platform where anyone can create and resolve markets.

name: Tug of MON
one_liner: 167 people tap their phones as fast as possible to pull a live rope — every tap batch settles on Monad in real-time, with a live TPS counter proving the chain is eating it
mechanic: Room scans a QR code, picks Red or Blue team. Everyone taps their phone screen frantically for 60 seconds. Each tap goes via websocket to a relay server that batches all taps into Monad transactions every 400ms (one block). The rope on the projector moves based on per-team tap differential. A live TPS meter on screen shows actual Monad throughput from the batch. Winning team's members claim a share of the loser pool on-chain after the round.
why_monad: 167 people tapping simultaneously generates hundreds of txs per second that must settle within one block to feel real-time. The live TPS counter on the projector directly visualizes Monad's 10k TPS capacity — the room sees the chain eating their input. Sequential EVM would create visible lag; parallel execution + 400ms blocks make the rope respond instantly.
room_participation: Everyone scans QR, picks a team color, and taps their phone screen as fast as humanly possible for 60 seconds. The projector shows the rope dragging in real-time, the live TPS counter spiking, and block confirmations rolling. The room screams for their team. Winner pot is claimable immediately.
build_plan_6h45: Contract: simple team-balance tracker + claim-winnings function (1h). Relay server: websocket tap aggregation, batched Monad tx submission via single relayer key (2h). Frontend: Next.js with animated rope SVG, QR join, live TPS feed from monode/Execution Events SDK, team counter (2h). Polish + demo dry run (1h). Stub: no anti-cheat, no persistent leaderboard.
biggest_risk: Wi-Fi can't sustain 167 concurrent websocket connections. Mitigation: relay runs on wired Ethernet, phones reconnect opportunistically, taps are idempotent (relay counts, on-chain only needs final totals).
novelty_vs_corpus: Hits three unbuilt white spaces simultaneously: mass-multiplayer live room game (4 built, 0 winners), room-joins-with-phone as core mechanic (0 built, 0 winners), and live TPS visualization (2 built, 0 winners). Tug-of-war is universally legible — zero explanation overhead.

name: Race the Chain
one_liner: A live TPS visualizer where the audience's transactions push a car toward the finish line, gamifying Monad's speed.
mechanic: A smart contract holds a global counter. Each audience member opens a web app and taps a 'Boost' button, which sends a transaction incrementing the counter. A frontend animation shows a car moving along a racetrack, its position proportional to the counter. The goal is to collectively push the car past the finish line within the pitch time. The current TPS is displayed prominently.
why_monad: Monad's 10,000 TPS and 400ms blocks allow the car to move smoothly with every transaction, demonstrating the chain's raw speed. Parallel execution ensures that hundreds of simultaneous boosts are processed without delays, making the race feel truly real-time.
room_participation: The presenter projects the racetrack. Everyone opens the app and starts tapping 'Boost' as fast as they can. The car accelerates, and the room cheers as it nears the finish line. The TPS counter spikes, visually proving Monad's performance.
build_plan_6h45: Smart contract: A single counter variable with an increment function. Frontend: Next.js with a simple canvas animation (car position = counter / target). Use a relayer with a single hot wallet to batch increments and avoid nonce contention. Stub: No complex game logic; just a counter and a visual. Use the monad-miniapp-template.
biggest_risk: Nonce contention if many users send from the same relayer wallet. Mitigation: Use a relayer that manages nonces internally, or have each user send from their own wallet with a small gas sponsorship. RPC rate limits could throttle transactions; use multiple RPC endpoints.
novelty_vs_corpus: Only two TPS visualization projects have been built, with zero winners. None turned the visualization into a live, room-wide game. This is a white-space concept that makes Monad's performance tangible and fun.

name: Trivia Burst
one_liner: Lightning‑fast live trivia where every phone answers a multiple‑choice question; correct answers earn MON instantly.
mechanic: A contract stores the current question hash and correct answer. At the start of the pitch the host reveals a 3‑second multiple‑choice question on screen. Attendees select an answer in the dApp; each selection is signed via Permit2 and submitted through a gas‑less EntryPoint. Monad processes all 167 answers in parallel, tallies correct responses on‑chain, and instantly distributes a small reward (e.g., 0.1 MON) to each correct participant. A leaderboard shows real‑time correct counts.
why_monad: Processing dozens of simultaneous answer transactions within seconds showcases Monad’s ability to handle high‑throughput, low‑latency events, emphasizing its 800 ms finality for instant reward distribution.
room_participation: During the pitch attendees read the question, tap their chosen answer button before time runs out, watch the on‑screen tally of correct answers, and claim their reward via a ‘Collect’ button after the round ends.
build_plan_6h45: - Contract: setQuestion(bytes32 hash, uint8 answer), submitAnswer(uint8 choice) with Permit2, tallyCorrect(), payout via Permit2. - Frontend: simple Next.js UI with question display, answer buttons, real‑time correct count via GhostGraph subscription. - Infra: sponsor wallet for payouts, use ERC‑4337 for gas‑less answers. - Stub: pre‑write a few trivia questions; use off‑chain script to set question hash before demo.
biggest_risk: Ensuring all answers are submitted before the deadline; mitigate by allowing a 5‑second submission window and batch processing. Possible RPC limits; use a single relayer contract to bundle signatures.
novelty_vs_corpus: Trivia/prediction games have decent win rates, but no prior Blitz project has made the audience’s phones the primary input for a real‑time answer‑tallying contest that resolves instantly on‑chain; this leverages peer‑rating by giving participants a tangible reward they earned live.

name: Monad Mural
one_liner: r/place at Monad speed: 167 people try to paint one giant Monad-London mural in 30 seconds.
mechanic: Scanning the QR opens a color palette and the same 32-by-18 canvas shown on the projector. Every touch submits a signed paint intent, so independent pixels settle together while fights over popular pixels visibly overwrite one another. The room receives a simple target, such as a purple Monad logo on a London skyline, and has 30 seconds to recreate it. At freeze, the contract computes a lightweight similarity score and permanently seals the resulting mural hash.
why_monad: A few hundred people dragging fingers can generate thousands of pixel writes in seconds, making unbatched execution and fast blocks central to the experience. Independent pixel slots exploit optimistic parallel execution, while contested pixels create an understandable visual contrast between parallel and conflicting state. A side panel shows each new block, confirmed paints, conflicted coordinates and finality time.
room_participation: Everyone scans the QR and paints continuously for 30 seconds, either cooperating on the displayed target or fighting to alter the most visible pixels before the mural freezes.
build_plan_6h45: Deploy a compact Solidity canvas contract storing palette indexes, pixel versions and paint events. Build a touch-first Next.js client and projector view with optimistic coloring followed by confirmation flashes. Use burner signatures, 24 round-robin relayers, two RPC providers and optional batches of up to four pixels if congestion threatens the demo. Stub NFT metadata, moderation, arbitrary canvas sizes and sophisticated image scoring.
biggest_risk: Wi-Fi or RPC limits could make optimistic pixels diverge from confirmed state; visibly distinguish pending paint, cap each client to ten updates per second and retain small emergency batches.
novelty_vs_corpus: Only one of 1,327 projects attempted a pixel canvas, and none made a synchronized whole-room paint storm plus execution-conflict visualization the pitch itself.

name: ParallelScore
one_liner: Lighthouse for Monad contracts: paste the address you deployed today, we fire real load at it from 150 funded wallets and hand you a 0-100 parallel-execution score — live leaderboard of every project in the room.
mechanic: You submit your contract address plus one write function and an argument template. Our disclosed load fleet — 150 pre-funded keys on our own hardware and our own dedicated RPC — fires ~300 transactions with disjoint parameters, and we measure how densely Monad's optimistic parallel execution packs them into blocks versus two calibrated baselines run identically: a fully-parallel independent-slots contract and a fully-serial hot-counter contract. You get a 0-100 ParallelScore, blocks-to-clear, and heuristic 'what serializes you' hints (shared counters, global totals, hot mappings). Every scored contract joins an on-chain leaderboard of the hackathon.
why_monad: This product is meaningless on any other chain — parallel execution IS the subject, not a backdrop. The proof is honest by construction: the load is explicitly ours and labeled as such on the slide ('150 of our keys, our RPC, fleet address list published'), and the metric is relative block-packing against baselines run the same way, verifiable block-by-block on monadscan. No audience TPS claims, no counter theatre — a benchmark with disclosed methodology, turned into a scoreboard the room competes on.
room_participation: Everyone in the room deployed a contract today. QR → paste your address → watch your score compute in ~20 seconds and your project slot into the live leaderboard during the pitch. Teams immediately compare scores with the next table — the pitch becomes the room benchmarking its own day of work.
build_plan_6h45: Contracts (1h): the two baseline contracts plus an on-chain Scoreboard. Load engine (2.5h): fleet funding script, tx-template builder from ABI (pulled via the monadscan API), firing and block-density measurement in viem. Frontend (2h): submit form, live score animation, big-screen leaderboard. Infra (0.75h): dedicated RPC, dry-runs against five common shapes (ERC-20 transfer, mint, counter, mapping write, game move). Stubbed: serialization hints are regex-over-verified-source labeled beta; contracts needing prerequisites fall back to a 'score my transfer path' mode; unverified contracts get score-only.
biggest_risk: Arbitrary contracts reverting under templated arguments — mitigated by supporting the five common shapes first, a pre-flight eth_call simulation of every template, and graceful 'we could not call this safely' messaging with the fallback mode.
novelty_vs_corpus: Nearest ancestor is Vertex, an OCC benchmark-infrastructure winner — but that was illegible infra; this converts the same physics into a consumer scorecard about the room's OWN work, the only pitch whose demo data is the audience's projects. Nothing in the 1,327 scores third-party contracts for parallelism, and dev tooling already outperforms baseline at 8.7%.

name: Pixel Rally Canvas
one_liner: Collaborative live pixel art canvas where each attendee can paint one pixel per second, creating a massive on‑chain mural in real time.
mechanic: The contract stores a 256 × 256 bitmap (uint8 per pixel). Attendees open the canvas UI, pick a color, and click on a pixel; the frontend signs a Permit2 permit for a single ‘paint(uint16 x,uint16 y,uint8 color)’ call, which is relayed via a gas‑less EntryPoint. Monad’s parallel execution handles thousands of concurrent paint calls, updating the on‑chain bitmap instantly. The UI streams the bitmap via monad‑monade SDK, showing the evolving artwork live.
why_monad: Updating a large bitmap with many simultaneous writes requires high parallelism; Monad’s 10k TPS and parallel execution ensure no write collisions and immediate visual feedback, a feat impossible on single‑threaded chains.
room_participation: Each participant chooses a color, paints a pixel on the shared canvas during the pitch, watches the collective mural grow, and can later claim a tiny NFT of the final canvas via a single click.
build_plan_6h45: - Contract: bitmap storage (mapping(uint16=>mapping(uint16=>uint8))), paint function with Permit2 verification, finalise() to mint NFT. - Frontend: React canvas UI, ethers.js, monad‑miniapp template, update via WebSocket from GhostGraph. - Infra: use QuickNode streaming for bitmap state, sponsor gas via ERC‑4337. - Stub: pre‑define a small color palette; skip NFT metadata generation if time low.
biggest_risk: State size limits if bitmap grows too large; mitigate by limiting canvas to 256×256 and restricting one paint per address per second. RPC load from many paint txs; use batch relayer to reduce calls.
novelty_vs_corpus: Pixel‑canvas projects are virtually absent (only 1 built, no winners). This idea makes the canvas the core interactive mechanic, leveraging the room’s phones to co‑create on‑chain art, a fresh take on the unbuilt white‑space.

name: ClapCeiling
one_liner: Over/under on how loud this room can clap—stage mic measures peak dB, Monad settles the pot.
mechanic: Host posts a target decibel (e.g. 92 dB). The room splits into OVER and UNDER by standing on opposite sides of the aisle—again, no phone txs for voting. A wired stage microphone feeds the Web Audio AnalyserNode; for five seconds the room claps while a live meter fills on the projector. When time ends, the stage wallet posts peakDb to the contract and the correct side claims the pot. Optional second round raises the target after the room has calibrated.
why_monad: Honest claim is timed resolution, not TPS. Betting lock, clap window, and oracle resolve are scheduled on block heights so the whole round fits inside a few seconds of wall clock. That cadence is the Monad pitch: the market is already paid out while people still have their hands in the air. Stage submits ~2–3 transactions; public RPC rate limits are irrelevant.
room_participation: Everyone picks OVER or UNDER by moving, then claps as hard as possible for five seconds while watching the live dB meter and the pot flip.
build_plan_6h45: Contract: ClapMarket with setTarget, lockSides, reportPeak, claim. Frontend: projector meter + host console (target, start, lock). Infra: stage laptop mic permission over HTTPS, one oracle wallet. Stub: host manually enters peak dB from a hardware meter app if browser mic fails; aisle choice can be host-entered.
biggest_risk: Venue mic gain/noise floor making absolute dB unreliable; use a relative calibration clap first, show a normalized meter, and let the host set the target from the calibration peak.
novelty_vs_corpus: Prediction/betting wins at 10.9% and IRL-sensor at 15.8%, but no winner used whole-room applause as the oracle. It is not Hunch (YES/NO on presentations), not Mojoman (pose reps), and not a phone-tap crowd game that dies on Wi-Fi.

name: Mini Agent Marketplace
one_liner: A lightning‑fast marketplace where each attendee hires a tiny pre‑built AI agent (e.g., a counter or timer) for a few MON, showcasing on‑chain agentic interactions.
mechanic: The contract hosts a catalog of 5 simple agents (e.g., CounterAgent, TimerAgent, RandomNumberAgent) each represented by an ERC‑4337 account with a predefined behavior script stored on‑chain. Attendees browse the marketplace UI, pay a 0.5 MON fee via Permit2, and the contract spawns an instance of the chosen agent bound to their address. The UI then shows the agent performing its task in real time (e.g., counting up, counting down, generating a random number). All agent calls are processed in parallel, allowing 167 agents to run simultaneously without lag.
why_monad: Running dozens of autonomous agents in parallel demonstrates Monad’s optimistic parallel execution; each agent’s state updates are processed in the same block, enabling real‑time feedback that would stall on single‑threaded chains.
room_participation: During the pitch each participant selects an agent, confirms the tiny payment, watches their agent’s output (e.g., a timer counting down) on the shared screen, and can interact (e.g., reset timer) via a button, reinforcing the perception of on‑chain AI.”
build_plan_6h45: - Contract: AgentCatalog with struct (price, codeHash), hireAgent(uint256 id) creates a new Agent contract instance, stores owner, simple logic per agent. - Frontend: Next.js marketplace UI, list agents, show live state via monad‑monade SDK. - Infra: sponsor gas via ERC‑4337, use QuickNode for event streaming. - Stub: implement only CounterAgent and TimerAgent; skip complex AI agents. Pre‑deploy agent bytecode libraries.
biggest_risk: Deploying multiple agent contracts could hit contract size limits; mitigate by using a minimal proxy pattern (CreateX) to point to shared logic. RPC overload from 167 concurrent state reads; use GhostGraph streaming to offload UI updates.
novelty_vs_corpus: Agent marketplaces have a ~9.7% win rate, but prior winners focused on specialist AI design agents. This idea flips the paradigm: simple, instantly understandable agents that every attendee can hire on the spot, turning the marketplace into an interactive demo rather than a background tool.

name: Monad Mosaic
one_liner: A collaborative on-chain pixel canvas where the entire room creates a giant artwork in real time.
mechanic: A 100x100 pixel grid is stored entirely on Monad. Each pixel placement is a transaction that sets a color at a coordinate. The canvas is displayed on the big screen. During the pitch, the audience is invited to open a web app, pick a color, and tap to place pixels, collectively drawing something like the Monad logo or a meme.
why_monad: Monad's high throughput and parallel execution allow hundreds of pixel placements per second without gas wars or congestion. 400ms blocks mean the canvas updates almost instantly, creating a smooth collaborative drawing experience that would be impossible on slower chains.
room_participation: The presenter projects the live canvas. Everyone opens the app on their phone, selects a color, and starts tapping. The room watches the artwork emerge in real time, with the most active contributors highlighted. The final mosaic is minted as an NFT commemorating the event.
build_plan_6h45: Smart contract: Simple Solidity contract with a mapping of (x,y) to color, and a placePixel function. Frontend: HTML5 canvas that reads the contract state and sends transactions. Use a relayer with a single hot wallet to batch pixel placements and avoid nonce issues. Stub: No complex indexing; read directly from contract events. Use the monad-miniapp-template for quick setup.
biggest_risk: RPC rate limits if 167 people send transactions simultaneously. Mitigation: Use a relayer that aggregates pixel placements off-chain and submits them in batches, or implement a commit-reveal with a short delay. Wi-Fi reliability is critical; a local fallback server could cache placements.
novelty_vs_corpus: Only one pixel canvas project has been built in 1,327 attempts, with zero winners. This is a pure white-space concept that turns the room into co-creators, not just spectators. It's visually striking and instantly understandable.

name: NADSASSIN
one_liner: The classic all-day hackathon game of Assassin, refereed by Monad: stake 1 MON, get a secret target, log kills by scanning your victim's QR, last nad standing takes the pot — every kill a real on-chain transaction.
mechanic: Join via QR at lunch: the browser generates an ephemeral wallet, our funder dusts it with gas, you stake 1 testnet MON into the pot contract and receive a secret target (another attendee). To make a kill you must physically find your target: their app shows a rotating signed 'death certificate' QR; scanning it lets your wallet call killTarget(victimSig) — the contract ecrecovers the victim's key, marks them dead, transfers their target to you, and emits a kill event. A live kill-feed and remaining-players counter runs on the venue screen all afternoon. At pitch time the final survivors are called on stage for a sudden-death scan-off and the winner's claim() pays the whole pot.
why_monad: Honest by design — zero throughput theatre: each kill is one ordinary transaction sent by the killer's own funded browser wallet at natural low rate across five hours, so public-RPC rate limits are never stressed and no relayer feeds any counter. What Monad visibly adds: sub-second finality makes the 'you're dead' moment land live in front of both players the instant the QR is scanned (on a 12s-block chain the kill confirmation is mush), and the explorer shows ~150 distinct player addresses that each genuinely sent their own stake and kill transactions — auditable by anyone in the room.
room_participation: They have been playing since 13:00, so the pitch is the season finale: the big screen replays the day's kill graph and most-wanted leaderboard, the last 3 survivors come on stage for a live sudden-death (first scan wins), and the pot pays out on-screen in under a second while everyone else looks up their own death record in the feed.
build_plan_6h45: Contract (1.5h): Assassin.sol — join/stake, ring-of-targets assignment, killTarget with ecrecover of victim cert, sudden-death mode, claim; deployed from the foundry-monad template. Frontend (3h): mobile web app — ephemeral viem wallet in localStorage, QR render + jsQR scanner, target card, kill-feed via log polling; separate big-screen spectator page. Infra (1h): gas-dusting funder script, dedicated free-tier RPC endpoint, printed QR posters at lunch. Stubbed: no proof-of-kill beyond the QR handshake, simple ring reassignment only, no bounty or revival modes.
biggest_risk: Cold-start adoption — if fewer than ~40 people join during lunch the finale feels thin; mitigated by aggressive 13:00 seeding (posters, walking the floor, calling out first blood on the screen) and the game costing players zero effort between builds.
novelty_vs_corpus: None of the 1,327 projects is an IRL elimination game. Nearest winner is Mojoman (spectators bet on others' exercise) — this is player-vs-player IRL with the phone camera as the weapon, in the best-performing category (IRL sensor/camera, 15.8% win rate, only 19 ever built), and the all-day deployment means the room has already touched it before they vote.

name: TapTug War
one_liner: Mass‑multiplayer tap‑the‑button tug‑of‑war where every phone’s tap pushes the rope and the winning side sweeps the MON prize.
mechanic: A minimalist contract tracks two counters, LEFT and RIGHT. During the 2‑minute pitch each attendee chooses a side on the UI and taps a button; each tap sends a tiny gas‑less transaction via ERC‑4337’s EntryPoint (using a shared sponsorship wallet). Monad’s optimistic parallel execution processes thousands of taps per second, updating the on‑screen rope position in real time. After 60 seconds the side with the higher count claims the pooled stake.
why_monad: The demo generates an intense burst of ~10,000 tiny transactions in seconds; only Monad’s parallel VM can keep the rope moving smoothly without lag, showcasing its high‑throughput advantage.
room_participation: Attendees select LEFT or RIGHT on the dApp, repeatedly tap the button for the duration of the pitch, and watch the animated rope sway; at the end they press ‘Collect’ to receive any reward if their side won.
build_plan_6h45: - Contract: two uint256 counters, stake function, tap() increments chosen side, end() resolves and distributes pool via Permit2. - Frontend: Next.js UI with tap button, side selector, animated rope using Canvas. - Infra: sponsor wallet funded with testnet MON, use ERC‑4337 to make taps gas‑less. - Stub: pre‑fund sponsor, mock final distribution if time runs out.
biggest_risk: Potential RPC throttling from 167 simultaneous meta‑transactions; mitigate by batching taps off‑chain and submitting aggregated signatures every few seconds. UI latency on some phones could reduce tap rate, but the visual rope remains engaging regardless.
novelty_vs_corpus: While ‘mass‑multiplayer live room games’ have been attempted, none have realized a real‑time tug‑of‑war with every phone as a core input; this flips the unbuilt white‑space into a simple, high‑energy, peer‑rated crowd game.

name: Ephemera
one_liner: On-chain chat room where messages vanish after a few minutes, turning the audience into live participants.
mechanic: A chat room where every message is an on-chain transaction with a timestamp. The frontend displays only messages from the last 5 minutes, creating an ephemeral feed. The room can be used for anonymous Q&A, jokes, or feedback during pitches. A simple spam prevention mechanism (e.g., a tiny MON fee) keeps it clean.
why_monad: Monad's 10,000 TPS and parallel execution allow a real-time chat experience with on-chain permanence. Messages are processed independently and appear in the feed within 400ms, making it feel like a Web2 chat app but fully decentralized.
room_participation: During the pitch, the presenter asks the audience to send messages to the chat. The big screen shows messages appearing and fading away. The presenter can respond to questions or highlight funny comments, creating a dynamic, interactive presentation.
build_plan_6h45: Smart contract: A simple contract storing messages (sender, text, block.timestamp). Frontend: Next.js app with a message feed that filters out messages older than 5 minutes. Use Privy for embedded wallets and a relayer for gasless transactions. Stub: No complex moderation; rely on the fee to deter spam. Use the monad-miniapp-template.
biggest_risk: Spam could overwhelm the feed if the fee is too low. Mitigation: Set a small but meaningful fee (e.g., 0.01 testnet MON) and implement a simple rate limit per address. Wi-Fi issues could delay message appearance; use optimistic UI updates.
novelty_vs_corpus: Chat/messaging projects have a 14.3% win rate, but none of the 1,327 past projects focused on ephemeral, room-wide participation during the pitch itself. This is a live social tool, not a generic messaging dApp.

name: FlashPoll
one_liner: Democracy by flashlight: the room votes YES/NO by torching the ceiling; stage cameras tally zones onchain.
mechanic: Host asks a binary question about the room (e.g. 'Will it rain MON?'). People vote YES by turning phone flashlights ON pointed up, NO by keeping them off—no app, no Wi-Fi, no DeviceMotion permission. A stage webcam divides the audience into 12–16 brightness zones. For three seconds the host shouts VOTE, then the stage machine signs one transaction per zone wallet reporting brightness. The contract aggregates YES/NO weight, and a side panel shows each zone's pending vs confirmed oracle tx. Optional MON pot pays the majority side if supporters deposited earlier from a few stage tablets.
why_monad: Honest parallel execution demo: 12–16 independent zone storage writes from distinct wallets in the same block(s), with a conflict-free aggregation read afterward. The projector proves it with a lane panel (zone id, tx hash, confirmed) rather than a single-relayer TPS cartoon. Sub-second blocks make the light map finalize while flashlights are still on.
room_participation: Every phone becomes a vote torch. The whole room goes dark/bright together, then watches their zone tiles flip from pending gray to confirmed green on the projector.
build_plan_6h45: Contract: FlashPoll with zoneReport(zone,bps), finalize, optional pot. Frontend: projector heat map + host question console. Infra: stage webcam, 16 prefunded zone signers on one laptop with local nonces, wired Ethernet. Stub: skip MON pot and only publish the onchain poll result; reduce to 8 zones if time is short.
biggest_risk: Ambient house lights washing out torch signal; kill projector wash on the audience, raise camera exposure threshold live, and allow a second VOTE take.
novelty_vs_corpus: Room-joins-with-phone as the core mechanic was listed as unbuilt white space, but prior attempts assumed every phone sends transactions. FlashPoll uses phones as dumb light sources and keeps all chain I/O on stage—so it survives the RPC/Wi-Fi facts that killed tap-storm ideas. No flashlight-vote winner exists in the 66.

name: Roshambo Royale
one_liner: 167 players, 8 rounds, 2 minutes, 1 champion: the world's fastest knockout tournament — rock-paper-scissors where every throw is signature-verified and every round settles on-chain in about a second.
mechanic: Everyone scans in before the pitch (browser key, auto-registered on-chain). The contract pairs all entrants; each round you get 10 seconds to throw rock, paper or scissors against your assigned opponent — the app shows their name so you physically look around the room for them. Both throws are EIP-712-signed; relayers submit the round's batch; the contract verifies both signatures per pair, resolves winners (ties broken by blockhash parity, disclosed up front), eliminates half the room, and instantly re-pairs survivors. The big screen shows the 167-leaf bracket collapsing live; after ~8 rounds one champion claims the MON pot on stage.
why_monad: The relay of signed throws is disclosed and the pitch never claims audience TPS — the claim is settlement cadence: a knockout of 167 people requires 8 strictly sequential on-chain rounds (verify ~160 signatures, resolve, re-pair) inside 120 seconds, a complete verified settlement every ~13s. With 400ms blocks each round confirms in about a second, leaving 10s of human think-time; on a 12s-block chain the bracket alone needs 8+ minutes with zero think-time. Per-round events name every winner and loser, auditable on the explorer the moment the pitch ends.
room_participation: Every single person plays every round until eliminated — finding their opponent across the room, throwing on their phone, watching their name die or advance on the giant collapsing bracket. Eliminated players stay invested in their bracket branch, and the champion is paid the pot live on stage.
build_plan_6h45: Contract (2h): Royale.sol — register, roundSubmit(pairs, sigs) with two ecrecovers per pair, resolve/re-pair logic, byes, no-show auto-fold, pot claim. Frontend (2.5h): phone throw UI with opponent card and countdown, big-screen bracket collapse animation driven by chain events. Relayer (1h): websocket sig collector, batch submitter, round timer. Infra (0.75h): dedicated RPC, 200-signer synthetic rehearsal. Stubbed: ties are blockhash parity rather than rethrow, single tournament instance, no seeding/rankings.
biggest_risk: Round pacing — a slow settle or Wi-Fi blip desyncs the countdown; mitigated by generous 10s windows, auto-fold for no-shows, and full rehearsal; worst case the bracket runs 3 minutes instead of 2, which is still a spectacle.
novelty_vs_corpus: No live human-vs-human tournament exists anywhere in the 1,327 (BLUFF was AI agents playing poker; Hunch was passive audience prediction). Rock-paper-scissors needs zero rules explanation in any language, and 'the fastest tournament ever run' is a one-screenshot claim with the bracket as proof.

name: Consensus Clash
one_liner: 167 people vs the blockchain: a live tug-of-war where every tap is a transaction.
mechanic: Room splits Left/Right. Tapping button signs tx incrementing team counter. Smart contract compares totals every block. Winning team splits pot.
why_monad: 167 concurrent writes to same state variables requires parallel execution to prevent nonce contention and failed txns on standard EVM.
room_participation: Everyone scans QR, taps repeatedly for 60 seconds while bar visualizes live on screen.
build_plan_6h45: Solidity counter contract + Next.js frontend using Privy for gasless. Off-chain relayer batches signatures to avoid nonce issues. Optimistic UI for instant feedback.
biggest_risk: Venue Wi-Fi collapsing under 167 simultaneous WebSocket connections.
novelty_vs_corpus: Zero prior mass multiplayer live room winners; shifts focus from individual skill to collective state contention.

name: BlinkOff
one_liner: Two volunteers stare on stage; MediaPipe detects the first blink; the room's left/right bet settles on Monad in one block.
mechanic: Two volunteers sit under a wired stage webcam running MediaPipe Face Landmarker with eyeBlinkLeft/eyeBlinkRight blendshapes. Before the stare starts, the projector splits the room into LEFT and RIGHT aisles and people physically move to bet on who blinks first—no audience transactions required. The stage laptop is the only RPC client: it opens the market, locks bets at a chosen block, posts the blink winner as oracle, and pays the winning aisle's pot. A big on-screen fuse counts down in blocks so the room sees the lock and the settlement land within about a second.
why_monad: The product is sub-second market lock + settlement, not a fake TPS meter. A stare contest only feels live if bet lock and payout finalize inside ~1–2 blocks; on a 12s-block chain the market would still be open after someone already blinked. The pitch shows block height, lock receipt, and payout receipt on the projector—typically three stage-signed transactions total, fully honest under public RPC rate limits.
room_participation: Everyone stands and walks left or right to pick a contestant, then watches the stare and cheers when the loser's eyes close and the aisle pot flips green on screen.
build_plan_6h45: Contract: BlinkMarket with open/lock/resolve/claim, aisle pools, and a single trusted stage oracle address. Frontend: Next.js projector page + volunteer face overlay using @mediapipe/tasks-vision FaceLandmarker. Infra: one funded stage wallet on wired Ethernet to a private/higher-limit RPC if available, else public RPC is fine at ~3 txs. Stub: skip per-wallet betting UI entirely; aisle occupancy can be a manual host toggle if camera headcount is unfinished.
biggest_risk: Lighting, glasses, or face angle making blink detection flaky; mitigate with a large blink threshold, a visible confidence meter, and a host override button that still settles onchain.
novelty_vs_corpus: Fitness/camera is the highest-win category (15.8%), but no recorded winner or prior London candidate is a stare/blink duel. Mojoman counted exercise reps; Proof of Jump mined whole-room motion; HeartChain's finger-PPG path is falsified on iOS. This is a new IRL-sensor mechanic with zero audience Wi-Fi dependency.

name: Hivemind Snake
one_liner: Twitch Plays Pokémon, live in the room: everyone's phone becomes a D-pad steering one game of Snake, and every 2-second move is a majority vote of signed ballots tallied and executed on-chain.
mechanic: Scan the QR and your phone becomes a controller backed by an ephemeral in-browser key. Every 2 seconds your latest direction press is signed (EIP-712 over game id, tick, direction) and a keeper submits the tick's ballot batch to the Snake contract, which ecrecovers every vote, tallies the majority, advances the snake one step fully on-chain, and emits the new board; the venue screen renders directly from chain events. Apples release 1 MON from the prize pool into a communal pot, crashes burn a life, and after three lives the final score — with every voter's address in the event log — is etched on-chain as 'London, 8 Aug 2026'.
why_monad: Architecture disclosed on the slide: phones sign, one keeper carries ballots — the why-Monad is the game loop, never a TPS meter. A 2-second democratic tick (collect → ecrecover ~150 signatures on-chain → move → render) needs blocks far faster than the tick: at 400ms Monad settles five blocks per move; on a 12s-block chain one move takes 12+ seconds and the game is literally unplayable. Every individual vote is signature-verified on-chain and queryable per address, so anyone in the room can find their own exact votes in the log after the pitch — verified mass participation, honestly framed.
room_participation: Their phones are the controller for the full 2 minutes: 150+ people mashing arrows, groaning at the hivemind's terrible decisions, cheering apples that visibly add MON to the pot, then pulling up the event log to find their own votes recorded on-chain forever.
build_plan_6h45: Contract (2h): SnakeGame.sol — board state, tick(votes[]) with batch ecrecover + majority + movement, apple placement from prevrandao. Frontend (2.5h): phone D-pad with key-gen and signing, big-screen canvas renderer reading chain events over websocket RPC. Keeper (1h): websocket signature collector, per-tick batch submitter with retry and timeout auto-advance. Infra (0.5h): dedicated RPC, full dress rehearsal with 200 synthetic signers before 18:00. Stubbed: single game instance, fixed pot-split rule, no cosmetics.
biggest_risk: Keeper/tick reliability on venue Wi-Fi — one stalled tick kills momentum; mitigated by the deliberately relaxed 2s tick, tick-timeout auto-advance, cellular backup for the keeper, and the synthetic-load rehearsal.
novelty_vs_corpus: The corpus shows 'room joins with phones as the CORE mechanic' at 0 built out of 1,327 — this fills that white space without being the dossier's named tug-of-war/pixel-canvas clichés: it is a structured game with individually-verified ballots in the Twitch-Plays format every developer already loves, a format absent from all 66 winners.

name: Bot Brawl
one_liner: Audience stakes MON on AI agents fighting in a visible arena; stake weight influences win probability.
mechanic: 4 colored bots on screen. Audience stakes on color. Contract calculates win % based on stake weight + random seed.
why_monad: Parallel execution handles simultaneous stake updates and agent state transitions without blocking.
room_participation: Audience stakes on their preferred bot color; cheers for their bot during live simulation.
build_plan_6h45: Solidity staking pool + Canvas frontend. AI logic stubbed as weighted random number generation based on pool size.
biggest_risk: Logic appearing too random; mitigated by visualizing health bars updating per block.
novelty_vs_corpus: BLUFF was agent personalities; this is agent performance driven by audience capital (Financialized Esports).

name: Signal Stream
one_liner: Ephemeral chat where messages cost MON and disappear after 10 blocks; price filters spam.
mechanic: Send message + payment. Message appears on big screen. Deleted after ~4 seconds (10 blocks).
why_monad: 400ms blocks make ephemeral messaging viable; cheap fees allow high volume without L2 bridging lag.
room_participation: Everyone sends a emoji or word; screen floods with paid messages instantly.
build_plan_6h45: Contract storing message hash + expiry block. Frontend listens to events. Use thirdweb for embedded wallets.
biggest_risk: Offensive content; mitigated by simple client-side blocklist + deposit slashing.
novelty_vs_corpus: Chat apps exist, but ephemeral + paid + big screen visualization creates Wall of Noise effect not seen before.

name: BlockRelay
one_liner: Two human relay lines race: each person must get an onchain PASS confirmed before the next teammate can run.
mechanic: Two teams of ~8 volunteers line up to two stage tablets (or one laptop + one phone) on wired/tethered links. Lane A and Lane B each have their own funded wallet. Runner N can only tap PASS after runner N-1's transaction has a receipt; the projector shows both lanes' hop receipts and a wall-clock timer. First team to confirm the final hop wins a preloaded pot. Because the two lanes do not share storage, their transactions can sit in the same blocks without conflict—shown as two receipt streams advancing side by side.
why_monad: This is a latency product with an honest parallel subplot. Serial hops make fast blocks visceral: eight hops at ~12s/block would take minutes; on Monad they finish during the pitch. Parallelism is proven by two independent lane wallets confirming in the same blocks on the explorer panel—not by batching 167 taps through one relayer into a fake TPS counter.
room_participation: Sixteen volunteers run the relay; everyone else picks a side by cheering/standing and watches hop receipts land live. Optional: aisle pots paid to the winning team's supporters via host-entered side totals.
build_plan_6h45: Contract: RelayRace with two lane nonces/hop indices, pass(lane), and finish. Frontend: dual-lane projector + big PASS buttons on two devices. Infra: two prefunded wallets, local nonce management per Monad best practices, wired Ethernet. Stub: skip supporter betting; hardcode 6 hops per lane if time is tight.
biggest_risk: Tablet Wi-Fi stall mid-hop looking like a chain stall; both lane devices must be wired or phone-tethered, and the UI must label 'waiting for receipt' vs 'rpc error' clearly.
novelty_vs_corpus: Not tug-of-war, not pixel canvas, not Proof of Jump's simultaneous crowd mining. No Blitz winner is a physical onchain relay race. It keeps room energy while staying inside a tiny, honest transaction budget.

name: BlockBeat
one_liner: GarageBand for the whole room: every phone becomes an instrument and every tap becomes an onchain note.
mechanic: The QR assigns each participant a colored instrument such as kick, clap, bass or synth. Taps play locally immediately, then quantize into a shared 16-step sequencer on the projector once their transactions confirm. For 30 seconds the audience collectively builds a beat while confirmed notes create colored rain grouped by Monad block. The finale replays the song solely from contract events and seals its event hash as the room's track.
why_monad: A musical crowd can create hundreds of notes per second, and keeping each note onchain requires throughput rather than a conventional batched NFT mint. Notes write to independent player and step lanes, matching parallel execution, while 400ms blocks provide a natural visible quantization unit. The screen reports notes per block, receipt latency and the exact event range used for the final replay.
room_participation: Everyone scans once and rhythmically taps their assigned instrument; the presenter conducts different sections of the room, then stops all live input and replays the confirmed onchain composition.
build_plan_6h45: Deploy an event-centric Solidity sequencer accepting signed note intents with song, step and instrument fields. Build a Web Audio controller and projector with four sampled sounds, server clock synchronization and block-event replay. Use WebSockets for immediate sound, 16 relayer lanes for settlement and preloaded audio assets so the chain is never in the audio-critical path. Stub editing, royalties, generative AI and full music production features.
biggest_risk: Unquantized crowd input can sound chaotic and network latency can confuse cause and effect; quantize aggressively, limit each phone's note rate and distinguish instant audio from confirmed visual locks.
novelty_vs_corpus: Past projects include games and NFT generators, but none use the entire room as a synchronized musical instrument whose final performance is reconstructed from Monad events.

name: FitBet Sprint
one_liner: Live group fitness challenge where attendees stake MON, their phone sensors count reps, and the fastest wins the pool.
mechanic: Each participant connects via a simple web dApp that accesses the phone accelerometer to count jump‑squats (or push‑ups). Before the 2‑minute demo window, everyone stakes 5 MON using Permit2. The contract aggregates counts in real time using Monad’s parallel execution and, after a 30‑second timer, instantly declares the highest counter and distributes the prize pool. A live leaderboard updates on screen as taps are recorded.
why_monad: Thousands of concurrent sensor submissions are processed within seconds; Monad’s 10k TPS and parallel VM guarantee zero‑lag tally even with 167 phones sending bursts of events. The finality within 800 ms lets the winner be shown instantly, a spectacle impossible on slower chains.
room_participation: During the pitch each attendee opens the dApp, grants a Permit2 signature, performs as many reps as possible in 30 seconds, watches the on‑screen leaderboard, and then clicks ‘Claim’ to receive any winnings.
build_plan_6h45: - Solidity contract: stake via Permit2, count(uint256 participant, uint256 reps) per tx, endTimer, payout logic. - Frontend (Next.js) using web‑sensor API, ethers.js, and monad‑miniapp template. - Infra: use Envio RPC endpoint, deploy to testnet 10143, mock sensor counts locally for testing. Stub: no AI, simple count aggregation. - Deploy contract early, hot‑reload UI during hack.
biggest_risk: Phone sensor permissions inconsistencies across browsers; RPC rate limits if all send txs simultaneously. Mitigation: batch counts via a relayer contract that aggregates off‑chain signatures before a single on‑chain submit.
novelty_vs_corpus: Fitness challenges have high win rate but never combined with real‑time sensor counts and on‑chain betting in a single room‑wide interactive demo; adds a tactile, audience‑driven core mechanic that no prior Blitz project has executed.

name: QuipChain Live
one_liner: Quiplash on Monad: the room writes punchlines, votes in a lightning bracket and crowns one immutable joke.
mechanic: The projector reveals one instantly legible prompt, such as the worst thing to hear from your smart contract. Audience members submit short answers for 20 seconds, after which four finalists enter two rapid head-to-head votes. Votes stream onto the screen as animated blocks without exposing interim totals on individual phones. A final ten-second vote crowns the room's winning punchline and mints it with its author and vote receipt range.
why_monad: The submission close and each vote opening create synchronized transaction bursts from the entire room. Separate voter-round storage allows parallel processing, and 800ms finality makes multiple verifiable rounds possible inside one short pitch. The projector shows confirmed vote totals, block hashes and finality while hiding pending totals to preserve the reveal.
room_participation: Everyone scans, types one short punchline, then taps between two large choices in each lightning vote; the winning joke is read aloud and its author is celebrated immediately.
build_plan_6h45: Deploy a Solidity game contract for timed submissions, finalist IDs, one-vote-per-session rounds and winner events. Build a mobile text-and-vote page plus a high-contrast projector bracket, using burner signatures and multi-lane relaying. Select finalists with a transparent seeded draw from valid submissions and apply only a basic local profanity list. Stub semantic moderation, token rewards, long tournaments and AI judging.
biggest_risk: Weak or offensive submissions can flatten the finale; use a safe prompt, strict character limit, profanity filter and seed two clearly labeled house answers only if fewer than four valid entries arrive.
novelty_vs_corpus: Chat is historically successful but rare, and the corpus has no whole-room comedy-writing game with rapid onchain brackets; it is neither a social feed nor a prediction market.

name: Pixel Paywall
one_liner: Competitive canvas where every pixel overwrite costs MON; last payer owns the color.
mechanic: 50x50 grid. Pay fee to change pixel color. Revenue accumulates in pot. Pot claimed by owner of most pixels at end.
why_monad: High contention on hot pixels requires parallel execution to process overlapping transactions without queueing.
room_participation: Everyone tries to paint a letter of MONAD simultaneously; screen shows chaotic color changes.
build_plan_6h45: Mapping contract (x,y -> owner) + Next.js grid. Use Envio for indexing state to frontend quickly.
biggest_risk: State bloat from 2500 pixels; mitigated by only storing changes/events not full state on-chain.
novelty_vs_corpus: R-Place was free/artistic; this is financial/competitive (King of the Hill mechanics).

name: HotPotatoMON
one_liner: One phone is the potato: pass it before the onchain fuse hits finality, or your seat burns MON.
mechanic: A single shared phone runs the web app and is physically handed around a row or circle. While you hold it, a contract fuse counts down in blocks (~2–3s). You must tap PASS (one transaction from the shared session wallet) and hand the phone to the next person before the fuse finalizes; if it expires on you, your pre-deposited stake is slashed into the survivor pot. The projector mirrors the phone UI: holder nickname, blocks remaining, last confirmed pass receipt. Only one device ever talks to the RPC.
why_monad: The fuse is the demo. A 2–3 second hot-potato only works when blocks and finality are sub-second; the same rules on Ethereum would give each holder half a minute of dead air. You prove Monad by projecting block numbers ticking on the fuse and the PASS transaction confirming before the phone reaches the next lap—not by claiming 10k TPS from one wallet.
room_participation: The nearest rows stand, form a pass line, and physically scramble the phone while the whole room watches the projector fuse; holders who get burned are called out by name on screen.
build_plan_6h45: Contract: HotPotato with join(stake), pass(toHint), burnOnExpiry, and pot claim for last N survivors. Frontend: mobile-first holder UI + projector mirror over websocket from the same phone session. Infra: one Privy/embedded or prefunded session key on the potato phone; stage Wi-Fi or tether for that single device. Stub: pre-register 12 volunteer names instead of open joining; skip NFT badges.
biggest_risk: Dropped phone or dead device mid-demo; keep a charged backup potato with the same session key restored, and a host RESET that starts a fresh fuse without blaming the chain.
novelty_vs_corpus: Zero hot-potato / pass-the-phone winners across 66 recorded Blitz winners, and none of the prior 22 London candidates used a single shared physical device as the entire network surface. It turns finality into a body game instead of a throughput theatre.
